title: What Makes a Disease Infectious? Classifying Pathogens: Bacteria to Prions
subtitle: What makes a disease infectious, and why does knowing which kind of pathogen causes it decide how it can be treated?
subject: Biology
lessonIntent: defining an infectious disease as one caused by a pathogen (most can pass between hosts), with tuberculosis against type 2 diabetes, and noting that most microbes are not pathogens; sorting pathogens by whether they are made of cells, and then whether they are many-celled animals, into microorganisms (bacteria, fungi, protozoa), macroorganisms (helminths, ectoparasites) and non-cellular pathogens (viruses, viroids, prions); describing each type's key structure with a named disease and its true relative size; distinguishing viroids (RNA only, known in plants) from prions (protein only, misfolding normal proteins, known in animals); showing the same groups in plants; explaining that a treatment must target something the pathogen has and the host lacks, so antibiotics act on bacteria but not on viruses or prions; classifying three unseen agents with justification and explaining an antibiotic's action on bovine TB but not BSE.

voiceover.text: In 1928, Alexander Fleming noticed a mould growing on one of his culture dishes. Around it, the bacteria had died, leaving a clear ring. That mould led to penicillin. But penicillin does nothing for the flu, for tinea, for malaria or for a tapeworm. So what makes a disease infectious, and why does the kind of pathogen decide how we can fight it?

An infectious disease is caused by a pathogen, an organism or agent that lives in or on another organism, its host, and harms it. Because the pathogen can pass from one host to the next, the disease can spread. Tuberculosis is infectious: a bacterium causes it, and it passes between people. Type 2 diabetes isn't. It comes from genes and lifestyle, so you can't catch it. And most microbes aren't pathogens. Your gut carries trillions of bacteria, and most do no harm, or even help.

Biologists sort pathogens with a few questions. First, is it made of cells? Bacteria, fungi and protozoa are single cells or fine threads of cells, each too small to see on its own, so they're microorganisms. Worms and ticks are animals made of many cells, usually big enough to see, so they're macroorganisms. Viruses, viroids and prions aren't cells at all. They're non-cellular, and they can only multiply inside a host.

Inside the microorganisms, ask a second question: does the cell have a nucleus? A bacterium doesn't. It's a prokaryote, with its DNA lying in the cytoplasm. The tuberculosis bacterium has a wall containing a material called peptidoglycan, and is a rod a few thousandths of a millimetre long. Fungi and protozoa do have a nucleus, like our own cells. Fungi grow as threads or yeast cells, with walls containing chitin, and spread by spores. Tinea, a skin infection, is caused by a fungus. Protozoa are single cells with no wall. Plasmodium, the protozoan that causes malaria, lives inside red blood cells.

Macroorganisms are parasitic animals. Helminths are parasitic worms, and many live inside the host. The pork tapeworm hooks onto the wall of the gut and can grow to several metres long. Other parasites live on the outside, like ticks and lice. Ecto means outside and endo means inside, so ticks are ectoparasites and tapeworms are endoparasites.

Now zoom in to a smaller example. A virus is genetic material, DNA or RNA, inside a protein coat. It has no cytoplasm and no ribosomes, so it can't make anything itself. It gets into a host cell and makes that cell build new viruses. The virus that causes COVID-19 is about a ten-thousandth of a millimetre across, so dozens would fit along one bacterium. Plants get viruses too, like tobacco mosaic virus, a rod of RNA in a protein coat.

Two non-cellular pathogens are even simpler, and easy to mix up. A viroid is just a small circle of RNA, with no protein coat. One makes potato tubers grow long and spindle-shaped. A prion is the opposite: a protein with no DNA or RNA at all. It's a misfolded copy of a normal protein found especially on nerve cells. When it meets normal copies, it makes them fold the same wrong way, like one bad apple spoiling the rest. Prions cause mad cow disease in cattle. So a viroid is RNA only, and a prion is protein only.

Plants are hosts too, and most of the same groups attack them. A bacterium causes crown gall, a swelling on stems. A fungus causes wheat stem rust. Tiny roundworms called root-knot nematodes swell plant roots into knots. And there are two exceptions to remember: the known viroids infect plants, and the known prions infect animals.

So why does the group matter so much? Because a drug has to hit something the pathogen has and the host doesn't. Antibiotics like penicillin act on parts only bacteria have, such as the peptidoglycan wall and ribosomes shaped differently from ours. A virus has neither, so antibiotics can't touch it, which is why they don't treat the flu. Fungi and protozoa have a nucleus like ours, so they need their own drugs, such as antifungals and antimalarials, aimed at their differences. And prions, with no genes to target, have no known cure.

Sort any pathogen in order. Is it made of cells? If so, is it a many-celled animal? Does it have a nucleus? And if it isn't a cell, is it RNA only, protein only, or genes in a coat? Then remember: not a cell means antibiotics are useless.

Two exam questions now. First. Three agents were isolated from diseased organisms. Agent P is a single cell with its own nucleus and no cell wall, found inside a bird's red blood cells. Agent Q is a small circle of RNA with no protein coat, from deformed potato tubers. Agent R is a flat, segmented worm two metres long, from a dog's intestine. Classify each agent, and justify each answer. Pause here to answer.

P is a protozoan, a microorganism, because it's one cell with a nucleus and no wall. Q is a viroid, which is non-cellular, because it's RNA with no protein coat. R is a helminth, a macroorganism, because it's a many-celled animal, a worm. Calling Q a small virus is the classic mistake: a virus has a protein coat.

Second. Bovine tuberculosis is caused by a rod-shaped bacterium. Mad cow disease, or BSE, is caused by a prion. Explain why an antibiotic could act on the pathogen causing one of these diseases, but not the other. Pause here to answer.

The antibiotic could act on the tuberculosis bacterium, because it's a prokaryotic cell with targets that only bacteria have, such as bacterial ribosomes and the enzymes that build its wall. The prion is a misfolded protein, with no cell, wall or ribosomes, so the antibiotic has nothing to act on. Saying the prion is too small for the drug to reach is the classic mistake.

So when a question names a disease, first ask what causes it: a pathogen, or something else. Then sort the pathogen with the four questions. Its group tells you what can treat it. Next, how scientists first proved that a particular microbe causes a particular disease.
